case_analysis.focal_point: Whether an order denying a federal contractor’s “derivative sovereign immunity” defense at summary judgment is immediately appealable under the collateral-order doctrine.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1291 (final-judgment rule) and the judge-made collateral-order doctrine (from Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp.).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: GEO Group argues that derivative sovereign immunity functions like an immunity from suit (not merely a defense to liability) when a contractor acts as the government’s agent under valid federal authorization, so denial of that protection should be immediately appealable as a collateral order to avoid the irreparable burden of litigation and to protect the federal government’s interest in having contractors perform delegated governmental functions without being deterred by protracted suits.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that a denial of derivative sovereign immunity is not a classic immunity-from-suit entitlement comparable to qualified immunity or sovereign immunity, but instead is a fact- and merits-bound defense tied to whether the contractor exceeded authority or violated law; because it can be reviewed after final judgment and because interlocutory review would expand the collateral-order doctrine and generate piecemeal appeals, such denials are not immediately appealable under § 1291.
key_precedents: Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp. (collateral-order doctrine)
CACI Premier Technology, Inc. v. Al Shimari, 141 S. Ct. 2850 (2021) (noted re: invited SG views on similar question)
Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction Co. (often cited source of “derivative sovereign immunity” for federal contractors)
Combs, 52 S.W.2d at 720 (state-law blasting case describing contractor as agent with immunity when non-negligent)
Nelson (Minnesota Supreme Court blasting/bridge case characterizing contractor as agent of the state and linking liability to the state’s)

John Roberts.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point is that Yearsley should be treated as an immunity from suit whose core benefit is avoiding the burdens of litigation, and thus a denial should be immediately appealable under Cohen. But as Justice Barrett emphasizes, Cohen’s separateness and effective-unreviewability requirements are not met because Yearsley turns on whether authority was “validly conferred” and not exceeded—questions typically intertwined with the merits and factual development, unlike qualified or sovereign immunity. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Campbell-Ewald further reinforces that contractors do not simply inherit the Government’s own immunity; the protection is conditional and evaporates when authority is exceeded, making it more like a liability defense that can be vindicated on appeal after final judgment. Given § 1291’s final-judgment rule and the institutional costs of inviting routine piecemeal appeals in contractor cases, I see no narrow, administrable basis to expand collateral-order jurisdiction here.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point is that Yearsley is functionally an immunity from suit whose value is lost if the contractor must proceed through discovery and trial, and thus should fall within Cohen. But as Justice Barrett persuasively emphasizes, Cohen is a narrow, judge-made exception to § 1291’s final-judgment rule and cannot be expanded to cover a defense that is intertwined with the merits—Yearsley turns on whether authority was “validly conferred” and whether it was exceeded, which often requires factual development. Campbell-Ewald, which I referenced and which Chief Justice Roberts also highlights, confirms contractors do not simply inherit the Government’s sovereign immunity; the protection is conditional and therefore any mistaken denial remains reviewable and remediable on appeal after final judgment. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers point further reinforces that we should not create new interlocutory appeal categories absent clear congressional authorization.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point is that Yearsley should be treated like an immunity from suit, so an erroneous denial is effectively lost once the contractor is forced through discovery and trial. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett stress, Yearsley turns on whether federal authority was validly conferred and whether the contractor stayed within it—questions intertwined with the merits and often fact-dependent, which fails Cohen’s separateness requirement and makes the issue reviewable after final judgment. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Campbell-Ewald further undercuts the “immunity” label because the protection evaporates when authority is exceeded, confirming it is conditional and not a categorical right to avoid trial. Given § 1291’s final-judgment rule and the systemic cost of opening a new channel for piecemeal contractor appeals, I see no textual or precedential basis to expand Cohen here.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point is that Yearsley is meant to spare contractors the burdens of litigation when they act under federal direction, so denial should be treated like an immunity-from-suit and immediately appealable. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan stress, Yearsley turns on whether authority was “validly conferred” and not exceeded—questions typically intertwined with the merits and factual development—so it fails Cohen’s separateness and “effectively unreviewable” requirements. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Campbell-Ewald further confirms this is not the Government’s sovereign immunity transplanted to private actors, but a conditional merits defense that can be fully remedied on appeal after final judgment. Pragmatically, recognizing collateral-order appeals here would predictably delay relief for injured plaintiffs through routine interlocutory appeals, undermining access to justice without clear congressional authorization to expand § 1291’s final-judgment rule.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point is that Yearsley should be treated as an immunity from suit, so the burden of litigation is itself the irreparable harm; but under Cohen, that kind of claim works only where the doctrine secures a freestanding entitlement not to stand trial. As Justice Barrett and the Chief Justice emphasize, the Yearsley inquiry—whether authority was “validly conferred” and whether it was exceeded—is typically interwoven with merits and factual development, so it is not sufficiently “separate” and any error is reviewable after final judgment. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Campbell-Ewald reinforces that contractors do not inherit the Government’s sovereign immunity categorically; the protection is conditional and evaporates when authority is exceeded, which is hard to square with interlocutory treatment. Given § 1291’s final-judgment rule and the predictable proliferation of piecemeal contractor appeals, I do not see a principled, textually coherent basis to expand the collateral-order doctrine here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point is that Yearsley is sometimes described as “derivative sovereign immunity,” and thus the right would be lost if a contractor must endure trial. But as Justice Barrett emphasizes, Cohen requires a truly separate, effectively unreviewable right, and Yearsley’s own terms hinge on whether authority was “validly conferred” and whether the contractor “exceeded” it—questions intertwined with the merits and often factual development. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Campbell-Ewald strengthens that conclusion: contractors do not simply inherit the Government’s sovereign immunity, and the protection evaporates when authority is exceeded, making it a conditional merits defense that can be corrected on appeal after final judgment. Given § 1291’s final-judgment rule and separation-of-powers limits on judge-made interlocutory categories, I see no warrant to expand Cohen here.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that Yearsley is styled as “derivative sovereign immunity” and therefore should be immediately appealable like qualified immunity to avoid the burdens of litigation, but that framing fails under Cohen because the asserted entitlement is not a freestanding right not to stand trial. As Justice Barrett persuasively explains, Yearsley’s core questions—whether authority was “validly conferred” and whether the contractor exceeded it—are typically intertwined with merits and factual development, defeating Cohen’s separateness requirement and making ordinary post-judgment review adequate. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Campbell-Ewald further undercuts petitioner’s characterization: contractors do not inherit the Government’s sovereign immunity categorically, so denial is not “effectively unreviewable” in the way true immunities are. Institutionally and practically, as the Chief Justice notes, expanding collateral-order jurisdiction here would invite piecemeal appeals across federal contracting and erode § 1291’s final-judgment rule without clear congressional authorization.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point is the “immunity from suit” characterization, but Cohen requires more than avoidance of litigation costs: it demands a right that is truly separate from the merits and effectively unreviewable after final judgment. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Yearsley turns on whether authority was “validly conferred” and whether the contractor “exceeded” it—questions tightly intertwined with merits and factual development—so it lacks Cohen separateness. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Campbell-Ewald strengthens this conclusion by clarifying that any derivative protection is conditional and evaporates when authority is exceeded, making it look like an ordinary merits-linked defense remediable on appeal. And, as Justice Gorsuch notes, absent congressional authorization we should be wary of judicially expanding § 1291’s final-judgment rule through a new collateral-order category for fact-bound contractor defenses.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that Yearsley is styled as “derivative sovereign immunity,” and thus a mistaken denial should be immediately appealable to avoid the burdens of litigation. But as Justice Barrett underscores, Yearsley’s applicability turns on whether the contractor acted within “authority validly conferred” and did not exceed it—issues typically intertwined with the merits and factual development, which fails Cohen’s separateness requirement. Chief Justice Roberts’ and Justice Kagan’s emphasis on § 1291’s final-judgment rule and the institutional costs of expanding collateral-order review is persuasive to me as a pragmatic matter: recognizing interlocutory appeals here would predictably generate routine piecemeal appeals in contractor cases. And Justice Thomas’s invocation of Campbell-Ewald reinforces my view that this is not a true inherited sovereign immunity (a right not to be sued), but at most a conditional defense to liability that remains effectively reviewable after final judgment.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1291 embodies a strong final-judgment rule, and under Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp. an interlocutory appeal lies only for a narrow class of orders that are effectively unreviewable after final judgment. Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction Co. describes what is often labeled “derivative sovereign immunity” as a merits defense to liability—turning on whether the contractor acted within validly conferred authority—not a nondelegable immunity from suit like Eleventh Amendment or other true sovereign immunities. Because a denial of a Yearsley defense can be reviewed after final judgment and is intertwined with merits and authority questions, recognizing collateral-order appealability would expand Cohen and invite piecemeal appeals inconsistent with institutional legitimacy and our repeated admonitions to keep the collateral-order doctrine narrow. The order therefore is not immediately appealable under § 1291.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1291 codifies the final-judgment rule, and the collateral-order doctrine of Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp. is a narrow, judge-made exception that should not be expanded beyond its established limits. Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction Co. is best understood as a merits defense tied to whether the contractor acted within valid federal authorization, not a categorical immunity from suit comparable to sovereign or qualified immunity; that characterization is reinforced by Campbell-Ewald Co. v. Gomez, which treats the protection as unavailable when the contractor exceeded authority and does not equate it with the Government’s own immunity. Because denial of a Yearsley defense is fact- and merits-bound and can be reviewed after final judgment, it fails Cohen’s requirement of an important, completely separate issue warranting immediate appeal. Allowing interlocutory appeals here would improperly broaden Cohen and undermine § 1291’s textually grounded preference for finality and against piecemeal appellate review.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. § 1291, interlocutory appeals are limited, and the collateral-order doctrine of Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp. applies only to a narrow class of orders that conclusively decide an important issue wholly separate from the merits and would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment. The so-called “derivative sovereign immunity” recognized in Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction Co. is best understood as a merits-linked defense to liability—turning on whether the contractor acted pursuant to validly conferred federal authority and within its scope—rather than a freestanding immunity from suit like qualified immunity. Because that issue is intertwined with factual and merits determinations and can be reviewed after final judgment, treating its denial as immediately appealable would expand Cohen and invite piecemeal appeals with substantial practical costs to the judicial system. Accordingly, the denial at summary judgment is not a collateral order immediately appealable under § 1291.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1291 embodies a strong final-judgment rule, and the collateral-order doctrine under Cohen is “narrow and selective,” requiring an order to resolve an important issue completely separate from the merits and to be effectively unreviewable after final judgment. A denial of a contractor’s Yearsley-based “derivative sovereign immunity” is not an immunity from suit like qualified immunity; it is a merits- and fact-bound defense turning on whether the contractor acted within validly conferred authority, so it can be reviewed after final judgment without irreparable loss. This Court’s cases caution against treating contractor defenses as sovereign immunity itself—Campbell-Ewald Co. v. Gomez makes clear that any “derivative” protection is limited and does not convert the defense into a right not to stand trial. Allowing immediate appeals here would invite piecemeal litigation across vast swaths of federal contracting, delaying remedies and access to justice for plaintiffs, including vulnerable individuals harmed by contractors’ conduct.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1291 embodies a strong final-judgment rule, and the Cohen collateral-order doctrine is a narrow exception limited to orders that conclusively decide an important issue that is separate from the merits and effectively unreviewable after final judgment. A Yearsley defense turns on whether the contractor acted within “authority validly conferred” and did not “exceed[] his authority,” 309 U.S. 18, 21 (1940), making it merits- and fact-bound rather than a freestanding immunity from suit like qualified immunity; errors can be remedied on appeal after final judgment. The Court’s treatment in Campbell-Ewald Co. v. Gomez, 577 U.S. 153, 166 (2016), reinforces that contractors do not “derive” the Government’s sovereign immunity from suit, supporting the conclusion that denial of a Yearsley-based defense does not satisfy Cohen’s “effectively unreviewable” requirement. Expanding collateral-order appealability here would invite routine piecemeal appeals across federal contracting, undermining § 1291’s workability and coherence.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1291 embodies a strong textual rule against interlocutory appeals, and Cohen’s collateral-order exception is a narrow, judge-made carveout that we have repeatedly refused to expand beyond truly irreparable “immunity from suit” interests. Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction Co. is best read as a limits-on-liability merits defense—turning on whether the contractor acted within validly conferred authority and followed federal directions—rather than an entitlement categorically not to stand trial, making it reviewable after final judgment without defeating any separate right. Because Yearsley’s application is fact- and merits-bound, allowing immediate appeal would invite piecemeal litigation and stretch Cohen beyond its strict criteria. Where Congress has not authorized such interlocutory review, separation-of-powers principles counsel restraint in enlarging appellate jurisdiction by judicial invention.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. § 1291 and Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp., interlocutory review is reserved for a narrow class of orders that conclusively decide an important issue separate from the merits and would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment. The protection GEO invokes from Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction Co. is best understood as a defense to liability that turns on whether the contractor acted within validly conferred authority and in conformity with federal direction—questions often intertwined with the merits and factual development at summary judgment. Because an erroneous denial can be corrected on appeal after final judgment and expanding immediate appeals here would invite piecemeal litigation, the order is not collateral-order appealable. Preserving the final-judgment rule’s workability and the Court’s restrained collateral-order doctrine counsels against creating a new category of immediate appeals for Yearsley denials.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1291 embodies a strong final-judgment rule, and the Cohen collateral-order doctrine is a narrow exception requiring an order that (1) conclusively determines the question, (2) resolves an important issue separate from the merits, and (3) is effectively unreviewable after final judgment. A Yearsley-based “derivative sovereign immunity” claim is best understood as a defense to liability—Yearsley itself frames the inquiry as whether the contractor “exceeded his authority” or whether the authority was “validly conferred,” 309 U.S. at 21—making the issue intertwined with merits and factual questions rather than categorically separate like qualified immunity. Because any error in denying the defense can be corrected on appeal after final judgment, the denial is not “effectively unreviewable” within Cohen’s meaning, and treating it as immediately appealable would expand interlocutory review beyond Cohen’s carefully cabined scope. Methodological consistency and precedent thus counsel adhering to § 1291’s finality principle and rejecting collateral-order jurisdiction here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under 28 U.S.C. § 1291, immediate appeal is the exception, and Cohen permits collateral-order review only for a narrow class of orders that conclusively decide an important issue completely separate from the merits and that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment. A denial of Yearsley/“derivative sovereign immunity” at summary judgment typically turns on whether the contractor acted within validly conferred federal authority and whether it exceeded that authority—questions that are intertwined with merits and factual development, making it a poor fit for Cohen’s separateness requirement. Unlike qualified immunity, which this Court has treated as an immunity from suit warranting interlocutory review in appropriate circumstances, Yearsley is better understood as a defense to liability that can be vindicated on appeal after final judgment without expanding piecemeal appellate jurisdiction. Prudentially, expanding collateral-order review here would invite fragmented appeals in contractor cases and undermine procedural fairness by delaying adjudication of serious statutory claims (including those involving coerced labor).

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a district court’s denial (at summary judgment) of a federal contractor’s “derivative sovereign immunity” defense is immediately appealable under the collateral-order doctrine rather than only after final judgment.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1291 (appellate jurisdiction over “final decisions” of district courts) and the judge-made collateral-order doctrine (as an exception to final-judgment review).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: GEO Group argues that derivative sovereign immunity functions like an immunity from suit (not merely a defense to liability) when a contractor acts as the government’s agent within valid federal authorization, and that forcing contractors to undergo discovery and trial before review irreparably defeats the protection; therefore, denials of the defense should qualify for immediate appeal as collateral orders to avoid chilling contractor performance of federal functions and to prevent the government’s work from being obstructed through litigation.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Menocal and the other respondents (supported by several amici and the United States) contend that derivative sovereign immunity for contractors is not a true, freestanding immunity from suit comparable to qualified immunity or state/federal sovereign immunity, but at most a merits defense that often turns on disputed facts about authorization and compliance; because it is intertwined with the merits and can be effectively reviewed after final judgment, it does not satisfy the strict requirements for collateral-order appeals, and allowing interlocutory appeals would expand § 1291’s narrow exception and generate delay and piecemeal litigation.
key_precedents: CACI Premier Technology, Inc. v. Al Shimari, 141 S. Ct. 2850 (2021) (referenced re: same issue and SG invitation)
Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction Co., 309 U.S. 18 (1940) (source of the “derivative sovereign immunity”/government-contractor authorization principle)
Combs, 52 S.W.2d 718 (Ky.) (state-law blasting contractor described as an “agent of the commonwealth” with immunity if non-negligent, referenced in amici discussion)
Nelson (Minnesota Supreme Court blasting/bridge case) (contractor characterized as state’s “agent,” referenced in amici discussion)

John Roberts.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point is that Yearsley is an immunity whose central benefit—avoiding the burdens of litigation—would be lost without immediate appeal, analogizing to Mitchell. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh stress, Mohawk and Digital Equipment require us to assess the category of orders as a whole, and denials of Yearsley protection typically turn on factbound disputes about federal authorization and compliance that are intertwined with the merits, defeating Cohen’s “completely separate” requirement. Justice Thomas’s framing further reinforces that Yearsley operates as a conditional defense tied to validly conferred authority, not a historically grounded, freestanding immunity-from-suit that is categorically “effectively unreviewable” after final judgment. A narrow holding refusing to expand collateral-order jurisdiction here best preserves § 1291’s final-judgment rule while leaving truly exceptional cases to certification or other established avenues.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point—pressed through the Mitchell analogy—is that Yearsley supplies an immunity from suit that would be destroyed by discovery and trial, but that characterization is not borne out by the doctrine’s structure or by §1291’s text. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, under Mohawk and Digital Equipment we must keep Cohen’s collateral-order category “narrow” and assess the class of orders as a whole; Yearsley denials typically turn on fact-bound questions about the scope of federal authorization and compliance that are not “completely separate from the merits.” On an originalist, textualist view, §1291’s “final decisions” rule controls absent a clearly established, historically grounded immunity-from-suit for contractors, and Yearsley reads instead as a conditional defense to liability that can be vindicated on post-judgment appeal. The availability of certification in exceptional cases further undercuts any need to enlarge a judge-made exception to the final-judgment rule.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point is the Mitchell-style claim that Yearsley is an immunity from suit whose core protection—avoiding litigation burdens—is lost absent immediate appeal, but Mohawk forecloses treating ordinary litigation costs as categorically “effectively unreviewable.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh stress, we must assess the class of orders as a whole under Digital Equipment, and Yearsley denials typically turn on disputed facts about the scope of federal authorization and compliance—issues intertwined with the merits and thus not “completely separate.” Justice Thomas’s framing reinforces my view: Yearsley functions as a conditional defense tied to validly conferred authority, not a historically grounded immunity-from-suit on par with sovereign or qualified immunity. Recognizing collateral-order jurisdiction here would invite routine piecemeal appeals by contractors and erode § 1291’s final-judgment rule, with exceptional cases better handled through certification or post-judgment review.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the Mitchell-style analogy: that Yearsley is an immunity whose value is avoiding trial and discovery, so denial should be “effectively unreviewable” later. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch explain, Yearsley turns on whether authority was validly conferred and whether the contractor stayed within it—factbound questions typically intertwined with the merits, failing Cohen’s “completely separate” requirement when assessed categorically under Mohawk and Digital Equipment (as the Chief Justice emphasizes). Even if litigation burdens are substantial, Mohawk rejects treating burden alone as enough to create a new collateral-order category, and expanding immediate appeals here would predictably delay relief for injured plaintiffs in a broad swath of contractor cases. Post-judgment review and targeted certification in the rare exceptional case are adequate safeguards without eroding the final-judgment rule and access to justice.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the Mitchell-style analogy: if Yearsley is an immunity from suit, the right is lost absent immediate appeal. But Chief Justice Roberts is right to anchor the analysis in Mohawk and Digital Equipment’s categorical approach: denials of Yearsley at summary judgment usually turn on disputed facts about the scope of federal authorization and whether the contractor complied, which is not “completely separate from the merits” and is adequately reviewable after final judgment. Justice Thomas’s framing also matters to me as a pragmatic textualist—Yearsley reads as a conditional defense to liability (authorized-and-within-scope), not a freestanding entitlement to avoid litigation, so the third Cohen factor is not categorically satisfied. Expanding collateral-order jurisdiction here would invite routine piecemeal appeals in contractor cases and erode §1291’s final-judgment rule without a sufficiently clear doctrinal or textual basis.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point is the Mitchell-style claim that Yearsley is an immunity from suit whose benefit is lost absent immediate appeal, but that framing overreads a conditional, fact-dependent defense as a freestanding immunity. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, under Mohawk and Digital Equipment we must evaluate the category of Yearsley denials, which commonly turn on disputed facts about the scope of federal authorization and compliance—issues intertwined with the merits and thus not “completely separate” under Cohen. Justice Thomas’s textual point reinforces my own: § 1291 codifies a final-judgment rule, and we should not expand a judge-made collateral-order exception absent a historically grounded immunity-from-suit right for contractors. Post-judgment review, with § 1292(b) certification in the rare clean legal case, is sufficient without inviting routine piecemeal appeals in contractor litigation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point—pressed most sharply as an analogy to Mitchell—is that Yearsley should be treated as an immunity from suit, so the right is lost absent immediate appeal. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Mohawk and Digital Equipment require us to assess the category of orders and keep Cohen narrow; Yearsley denials are typically factbound disputes about the scope of federal authorization and compliance, intertwined with the merits and therefore not “completely separate.” Justice Thomas’s framing is also persuasive on my methodology: Yearsley reads as a conditional merits defense to liability rather than a historically grounded, freestanding entitlement to avoid trial, making post-judgment review generally adequate under § 1291 (with certification available in rare cases). I therefore see no principled basis to expand collateral-order jurisdiction here without undermining the final-judgment rule and inviting routine piecemeal appeals in contractor litigation.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the Mitchell analogy—that Yearsley is an immunity from suit whose benefits are lost absent immediate appeal—but, as Chief Justice Roberts explains relying on Mohawk and Digital Equipment, litigation burdens alone do not justify enlarging Cohen’s “small class,” and we must assess the category of Yearsley denials in the aggregate. Categorically, Yearsley denials often hinge on fact-bound questions about the scope of federal authorization and whether the contractor complied, which (as Justice Kavanaugh notes) are commonly intertwined with the merits and thus fail Cohen’s “completely separate” requirement. Justice Thomas’s framing is methodologically decisive for me: on a textualist reading of § 1291’s “final decisions,” Yearsley functions as a conditional defense to liability tied to validly conferred authority, not a freestanding historical immunity from suit irretrievably lost by proceeding to trial. Post-judgment review therefore remains adequate in the ordinary case, with certification available for the exceptional one, so I do not see a sound basis to expand collateral-order jurisdiction here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point is that Yearsley operates like an immunity whose value is avoiding trial, but as Chief Justice Roberts notes (citing Mohawk and Digital Equipment), litigation burdens alone do not make a category of orders “effectively unreviewable” after final judgment under Cohen. I also find Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett persuasive that Yearsley denials typically turn on disputed, fact-bound questions about the scope of federal authorization and compliance—issues intertwined with what happened and therefore not “completely separate from the merits” in the categorical way collateral-order doctrine demands. Treating these denials as immediately appealable would invite routine piecemeal appeals in contractor cases, delaying adjudication for plaintiffs and undermining the final-judgment rule without a clearly established, freestanding entitlement not to be tried. Post-judgment review, with certification available in truly exceptional cases, is sufficient.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1291 embodies the final-judgment rule, and this Court has repeatedly insisted the collateral-order doctrine remain a “narrow” and “stringent” exception, not one that “swallow[s] the general rule.” Mohawk Industries, Inc. v. Carpenter and Digital Equipment Corp. v. Desktop Direct require evaluating the category of orders as a whole and demand satisfaction of all three Cohen factors; denials of a Yearsley/derivative-sovereign-immunity defense often turn on disputed facts about the scope of federal authorization and compliance, making the issue insufficiently “completely separate from the merits.” Because any error can generally be corrected on appeal after final judgment (with other mechanisms like certification available in exceptional cases), the asserted protection here does not justify expanding collateral-order jurisdiction in a way that would invite piecemeal appeals and undermine institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1291 provides appellate jurisdiction only over “final decisions,” and the collateral-order doctrine is a narrow, judge-made exception that should not be expanded beyond its established limits. The defense described in Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction Co., 309 U.S. 18 (1940), is best understood as a merits-related defense to liability turning on whether the contractor acted pursuant to validly conferred federal authority and within its bounds, not a freestanding immunity from suit akin to sovereign or qualified immunity. Because that inquiry overlaps with the merits and can be reviewed effectively after final judgment, it does not fit the strict collateral-order criteria derived from Cohen v. Beneficial Indus. Loan Corp., 337 U.S. 541 (1949). Treating such denials as immediately appealable would further erode the final-judgment rule in § 1291 and invite piecemeal appeals.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1291 limits appellate jurisdiction to “final decisions,” and this Court has repeatedly emphasized that the collateral-order doctrine is a narrow, judge-made exception not to be expanded simply because interlocutory review would be convenient. Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction Co., 309 U.S. 18 (1940), is best understood as establishing a merits principle that a contractor is not liable when it acted within “authority validly conferred” and did not exceed that authority—an inquiry that often overlaps with disputed facts central to the merits and can be reviewed after final judgment. Unlike qualified immunity or sovereign immunity, Yearsley does not clearly confer a freestanding right to avoid trial in all events, and allowing immediate appeals here would invite delay and piecemeal litigation contrary to § 1291’s structure and Cohen’s strict requirements. Practical consequences also counsel against enlarging collateral-order appeals in ordinary contractor litigation, which would burden courts and impede timely adjudication without the clear textual basis present for true immunities.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1291’s final-judgment rule admits only a narrow collateral-order exception, and this Court has repeatedly refused to expand it where the asserted protection is not a true immunity from suit and is intertwined with the merits. Yearsley is best understood as a merits defense that a contractor cannot be held liable when it acted pursuant to validly conferred federal authority and within its scope—an inquiry that often turns on disputed facts about authorization and compliance—making it ill-suited for immediate appeal under Cohen and this Court’s restrictive collateral-order cases (including Mohawk). The Court has also rejected the premise that contractors “derive” the sovereign’s immunity from suit, emphasizing that sovereign immunity “does not extend to those that act[] in its name,” which undercuts treating a Yearsley denial like qualified immunity. Allowing interlocutory appeals here would invite delay and piecemeal litigation in a vast universe of federal contracting, with particular harm to plaintiffs alleging serious abuses who need timely access to discovery and adjudication.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1291 embodies the final-judgment rule, and the collateral-order doctrine is a "narrow" exception that must remain of "modest scope" and "never be allowed to swallow" the rule. Mohawk Industries, Inc. v. Carpenter, 558 U.S. 100, 106-07 (2009). A denial of a Yearsley/derivative-sovereign-immunity defense at summary judgment typically turns on disputed questions of federal authorization and compliance, making it neither "completely separate from the merits" nor categorically "effectively unreviewable" after final judgment under Cohen’s three-part test. Because any error can be corrected on appeal after trial and allowing interlocutory appeals here would invite delay and piecemeal litigation beyond § 1291’s design, the order is not immediately appealable.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1291 authorizes appeals from “final decisions,” and the collateral-order doctrine is a “narrow exception” reserved for orders that conclusively resolve an important issue separate from the merits and are effectively unreviewable after final judgment. Digital Equipment Corp. v. Desktop Direct, Inc., 511 U.S. 863, 868 (1994). A Yearsley “derivative sovereign immunity” claim typically turns on whether the contractor acted within valid authorization and direction—questions entangled with what the contractor did (the merits) and often dependent on disputed facts at summary judgment. Unlike qualified immunity in Mitchell v. Forsyth, 472 U.S. 511 (1985), which is treated as an immunity from suit and thus effectively lost if trial proceeds, Yearsley is best understood as a merits defense to liability reviewable after final judgment; expanding interlocutory appeals here would stretch § 1291 beyond its settled limits and invite piecemeal litigation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1291 embodies the longstanding final-judgment rule, and this Court has repeatedly insisted that the collateral-order doctrine remain a “narrow” and “stringent” exception rather than a vehicle for piecemeal appeals. Under Cohen’s third requirement as applied in Digital Equipment and Mohawk Industries, the relevant “class of claims” here—Yearsley-style derivative sovereign immunity for contractors—does not generally confer a freestanding immunity from suit that is “effectively unreviewable” after final judgment, because it commonly turns on factbound questions of authorization and compliance intertwined with the merits. Unlike qualified immunity or sovereign immunity (which protect the sovereign or officials from the burdens of litigation itself), a contractor’s Yearsley defense can be adequately vindicated on appeal after final judgment, and expanding collateral-order review would risk the very delay and fragmentation § 1291 aims to prevent. Consistent with institutional concerns and workability, I would decline to enlarge the collateral-order category absent clearer historical grounding that Congress or this Court has treated contractor derivative immunity as an immediate-appeal right comparable to true immunities from suit.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1291’s text limits appellate jurisdiction to “final decisions,” and the collateral-order doctrine is a “narrow” exception that applies only when an order conclusively resolves an important issue separate from the merits and is effectively unreviewable after final judgment. Under Mohawk Industries, Inc. v. Carpenter and Will v. Hallock, we assess the class of orders and whether post-judgment review and other mechanisms suffice; denials of Yearsley-based derivative sovereign immunity commonly turn on fact-bound questions of authorization and compliance that are intertwined with the merits and can be remedied after final judgment. Unlike qualified immunity in Mitchell v. Forsyth—an established immunity from suit—Yearsley operates at most as a defense to liability conditioned on acting within valid federal authority, and recognizing immediate appeal here would expand collateral-order review beyond its methodologically consistent limits.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1291’s final-judgment rule admits only a “small class” of collateral orders, and this Court has repeatedly cautioned against expanding that exception beyond true immunities that would be lost if a defendant is forced to stand trial. Yearsley’s government-contractor protection is best understood as a conditional merits defense turning on authorization and compliance, often fact-bound and intertwined with the merits, which makes it unlike qualified immunity in Mitchell v. Forsyth and unlike sovereign immunity recognized as immediately appealable in Puerto Rico Aqueduct. Under Mohawk Industries v. Carpenter, litigation costs and discovery burdens—without a clear, freestanding entitlement not to be tried—do not render an order “effectively unreviewable” after final judgment. Allowing interlocutory appeals here would invite delay and piecemeal litigation in a broad swath of contractor cases, undermining procedural fairness and efficient resolution without a sufficiently weighty, categorical right to immediate review under § 1291.
